analysis.one_liner: Requires private health insurers to cover COVID-19 testing and treatment with no patient cost-sharing.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on March 11, 2020, sent to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: As COVID-19 first spread across the US, this bill would have required every private health plan to pay for COVID-19 tests, hospital care, vaccines, and related treatment without charging patients copays or deductibles. It would also have opened a special sign-up window so anyone diagnosed with COVID-19 could enroll in health coverage immediately, rather than waiting for the annual open enrollment period. The bill went to the Senate Finance Committee and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: People with private insurance who got sick with COVID-19 would have paid nothing out of pocket for testing, hospital stays, drugs, and vaccines. People without coverage who were diagnosed with COVID-19 could have enrolled in a plan immediately instead of being locked out until the next open enrollment, and uninsured patients would have had a route to coverage before their bills piled up.

how_it_helps.text: Every private health plan would have to cover outpatient and inpatient COVID-19 services, diagnostic tests, supportive care, vaccines, and related prescription drugs and medical devices, with no cost-sharing, for plan years starting January 1, 2020.

A person diagnosed with, or presumed to have, COVID-19 would get a special enrollment window to sign up for coverage through the marketplace, an exchange, or an employer plan, effective immediately upon diagnosis rather than waiting for annual enrollment.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers, and employers who fund health plans, would bear the cost of paying for COVID-19 testing and treatment with no patient copays or deductibles. Patients would bear nothing directly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer health plans

drawbacks.text: The mandate lands on private insurers and employer-sponsored plans, so premiums and employer benefit costs would likely rise to cover it — a cost that would partly flow back to workers through premiums and wages.

The bill did nothing for people with no plan to enroll in beyond the diagnosis-based enrollment window, and it left COVID-19 care outside private coverage (the uninsured who did not enroll) unaddressed.

It was a one-disease mandate with retroactive application to plan years already underway in 2020, which insurers would have objected to as a costly mid-year requirement without offsetting federal funding.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a national emergency, eliminating patient cost-sharing for testing and treatment directly removes the financial barrier that made people delay care, and the diagnosis-based enrollment window fixes a real gap for the uninsured. The trade-off is that the cost is placed entirely on insurers and employer plans with no federal subsidy, meaning some of it would return to workers as premiums, and it is narrow: it addresses one disease and leaves the fully uninsured largely untouched.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it sat until the Congress ended, so it never got a hearing or a vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker, joined by Sen. Robert Menendez, introduced the bill on March 11, 2020, as the COVID-19 pandemic was declared.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day; the bill received one cosponsor.
No further action was taken in the committee, and the bill died there when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer health plans came out ahead: the requirement to pay for COVID-19 care without patient cost-sharing never became law, so they continued to apply deductibles and copays as each plan's terms allowed, and patients who got sick kept facing those costs.

for.name: Sen. Cory A. Booker
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring free COVID-19 coverage and diagnosis-based enrollment windows.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-IA)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes on the bill, and the only listed supporters were its two Democratic senators, so no roll-call record shows a partisan split.

industries.note: The bill would have forced insurers and self-insured employer plans to pay all COVID-19 testing and treatment costs themselves, with no patient cost-sharing, including retroactively for 2020 plan years. The bill died in committee, so insurers kept applying deductibles and copays to COVID-19 care.

industries.industry: Employers that fund group health plans
industries.note: Employer-sponsored plans were subject to the same no-cost-sharing mandate and would have absorbed higher claims costs, though much of that would ultimately flow back to workers through premiums and wages.

Guaranteed coverage of COVID-19 diagnosis and inpatient and outpatient care would have meant more bills paid rather than absorbed as bad debt, and coverage accessible at diagnosis would bring patients in earlier.
